utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Sebastiaan van Hooydonk for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. It seems I'm not wide awake yet. For the Stanisic Defence team, Slobodan Cvijetic and Deirdre Montgomery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. May we go into closed session so the witness could be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I invite Ms. Korner to wind up her cross-examination, I remind you, sir, of the solemn declaration that you made when you first began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to the video we are looking at yesterday of the men we suggest were being led towards the sawmill by a special police officer. You've identified him as a special police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I think what we've done now is print off a still from the video which, Your Honours, we've arranged for hard copies to be given to everybody and one for the witness. But it's got the ERN number 0704-7618. So it can come up in e-court as well. I'm also going to ask that Your Honours be given and the witness have back the hard copy version of the photo-board of the special police which -- I've forgotten what the exhibit number was. P2417. And if Your Honours go in that, because it's easier to do this, to page with the ERN number 06785416, together with the still. Right. If I could ask the witness be handed that -- the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, it wasn't -- and I accept entirely it wasn't that easy when you were watching the video to identify the man, but are you now able to confirm that that special policeman leading those men is, in fact, the man you knew as Tomislav Miljkovic?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him as a fat man. This may be due to technical reasons, but he looks much slimmer here. So I cannot be certain that this is him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forget about the size of him. The face. Looking at his face. It's a -- it's a fairly good, I would suggest, depiction of face. Is that him, as he was in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to remember what he looked like in 1992. I remember him from the time when he was prosecuted for some crime. And I know that he was -- well, chubby.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if he looked like this in 1992, as I said, he wasn't anything like slim at the time when I -- from which I remember him, and he was being prosecuted for some criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that criminal offence rape?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or murder?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well I --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a robbery. The robbery of a gas station or something, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Overall, as a proportion of the police population, would you say there were a greater collection of criminals within the special police?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that there weren't many. We're talking about individual cases. And, funnily, this one was discovered and ended up in jail. Most people, most members of the unit, were conscientious men and didn't commit offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on because I have just got three other matters I'd like to deal with you. I'd like to go back to the video, please, P2014, and just play you a part of Mr. Ecim talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we can -- on the screen, sorry. Thanks. We seem to have lost... sorry. Do we have any sound?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Another Ustasha stronghold in Kotor Varos municipality has fallen and the commander of the special detachment of the CSB Banja Luka, Ljuban Ecim, will tell us how the action went. "This was certainly one of the most organised and best synchronised actions in the area of Kotor Varos. In six hours, excellent results were achieved. I would especially like to point out the assistance of the active-duty members of the CSB and they really lived up to the name of Krajisnik. We were able to destroy the core forces of the HVO with only one casualty on our side and three wounded."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we stop. I don't think the interpreter is keeping up. There is a transcript of is because certain words have been missed out. The transcript is at P -- tab 60. So I'd like to go back and start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand that the interpreters don't have a hard copy of the transcript, which is part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. In which case, let me hand -- I see, it's already gone to them. Where -- apparently, it was given -- it was handed in this morning. Yesterday. So they should have it. This is what causes delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But is the transcript an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it's, Your Honours. But you can't put it up at the same time as playing the video. In any event, already. Let's just play it through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] [As read] "Finally, another Ustasha stronghold in the Kotor Varos municipality has fallen. We're talking about the Kotor local commune. Ljuban Ecim will tell us more. "Ljuban Ecim: This was certainly one of the best organised and best synchronised actions in Kotor Varos municipality. In only six hours, excellent results were achieved. We have received excellent assistance from the reserve forces and the active forces of the Security Services Centre, many of whose members took part in combat for the first time today but truly up to the name of Krajisnik in battle. We were assisted by a certain segment of units of Serbian forces, Serbian troops of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. With only one victim and three wounded on our side, we managed to destroy the core of the HVO and kill the self-proclaimed HVO commander, Stipo Maric, also known as Sprzo, who has up until now inflicted heavy losses on us from many treacherous ambushes. His victims include Colonel Milan Stevilovic and head of our police department, Stevan Markovic ... came to collect its dues, and today we destroyed the entire group and liberated a larger portion of the town so that now it can be said that the entire city of Kotor Varos is finally free."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all I need. Your Honours, in the transcript it wasn't translated, but I heard the word, and I would be grateful if the witness could confirm it, or not I heard the words, I read the words: Excellent results were achieved in some six hours of action under the guidance of the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear those word, sir, said by Mr. Ecim?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it in the video-clip, but we need a complete translation to understand what this is about. This is a confirmation of the statement that the special detachment was outside the CSB because their staff were included for the first time. The complete translation will tell you all about it, and that's what I have been saying all along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But what it doesn't say -- what Mr. Ecim is not saying is that this unit was part and parcel of the military, because he specifically, as you say, says that there was assistance from the Serbian troops of the republic. Didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was speaking about the action itself. It was one action of many. And we can see who took part. Everybody participated. And he distinguishes between the participation of people from the CSB, on the one hand, and the special unit on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The whole thrust of your evidence, sir - this is the last time I want to deal with this - is this special police unit was nothing more nor less than a unit of the military under military command. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it was subordinate all the time, that they were under the military in terms of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, two other matters. First of all, you talked about the Doboj component of the special police, and you said that they were seconded to Doboj CSB and therefore the CSB Banja Luka had nothing to do with them. Is that -- is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were seconded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So do you have any explanation as to why the -- the request for payment of their salaries should be sent to the Banja Luka CSB?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was because the headquarters of the unit was there, and, thus, they could be paid. They weren't in one place all the time. They were moving in groups of five. They took shifts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, you explained to us. So, in other words, the unit that went to Doboj also went to other places and was also being paid by the CSB Banja Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that the Banja Luka CSB paid the ones who were in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the other way around. The Doboj paid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm not going to trouble to show you the actual document. But there's a document that shows that a request for payment was sent to the Banja Luka CSB. Now -- and what you're saying they would have no responsibility for paying them, would they?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, if somebody is seconded, then the one to whom they are seconded should pay and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I drafted a request for somebody to be paid because, by mistake, he wasn't on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You did; Mr. Kalamanda. However, that's the point, sir, that I'm making. They're not seconded at all, are they? They still come under the authority of the Banja Luka CSB, and they were merely sent off to do an operation in Doboj. That's the reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were transferred there for use.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want, then, to finally deal with one last document, on whether or not the CSB -- whether or not the special police were, in reality, disbanded on the 10th of August and sent to the military. Could you have a look, please, at P1666.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to remind myself what the tab number is. It's tab 38. Now, Your Honours, our markings say this is under seal. But I -- it's one of the documents that I think needn't certainly be under seal. I don't know whether ... so I don't know what the situation is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- we'll proceed if there is -- if there's anything that would comprise the witness then we'd not publish the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It has got nothing to do with the witness at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was under seal. It must have come in, I can't remember now, through another witness who was in closed session. But there is no reason, on the face of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the status still is as under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Until, yes, Your Honours have lifted the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so we'd lift it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'd lift it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there is a 1st Krajina Corps report dated the 29th of August 1992. And let's go to -- in English, over the page, this is under paragraph 4. And it will be over the page in B/C/S: "The Banja Luka CSB special detachment located in Kotor Varos area has still not joined the 22nd Light Brigade and is causing serious problems on the ground." Now, earlier, yesterday, I showed you the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff report for, I think it was the 23rd of August [indiscernible] and now this one. It's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just finish the question. It's right isn't it, sir --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just let me finish, please. It's right, isn't it, sir, that the special police brigade were not disbanded on the 10th of August and continued to commit crimes in Kotor Varos until the end of August, at least?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put up this document because you're showing something wrong to me. And what you're saying is not correct. This is not the document you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry? This is -- we'll go back to the front -- I'll give you the actual B/C/S copy and you can have a look at it. The part I'm just referring you to is the last part of paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm. This is obviously a military problem. We completed all payments on the 31st of August and had no more authority over them. It's a fact that at the time a number of people went to other units on their own and regulated their status. It can be verified that they received -- that they found positions in some other light units and had no more ties with the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, sir. You misunderstand, whether deliberately or not, I don't know, but you've been asserting that, certainly from the 10th of August and, indeed, before the special police were no longer in operation as a unit. I am saying to you from the evidence of the documents that the special police actually continued to operate certainly until the end of August. Now, there's a simple answer, either you say yes or no, you don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have that back, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, this: You said at page 25539 of the transcript, which was on the -- Thursday of last week, that: "I know in that period," this is at line 9, "there were many fighters who got killed or were wounded in both our ranks and theirs. There was sniper activity on a daily basis from the opposite side." Do you accept, sir, that in Kotor Varos, in which you were, the casualties on the other side, of civilians, in particular, were far, far greater than anything suffered by either the troops or, indeed, your special police?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated once that only on one occasion I saw dead bodies and that was when I was called to identify our fallen soldiers in the morgue. I didn't see anybody killed up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked there on several occasions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not what I'm asking you, sir. I'm not asking you what dead bodies you saw. I appreciate you're going back and back to that video that you're so keen on. But what I'm asking you is, as a matter of record, and at the time, were you aware of the hundreds of killed in attacks on villages and other areas?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You see, let's just look --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were stories about war going on. But, really, I am not aware of any mass murders of civilians. I really don't know anything about that. Because there were stories about fighting between our units of and units under the command of a person called Sprzo. They were also armed. Those are military activities, fighting between equals on both sides, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You know perfectly well, sir, don't you, this wasn't even remotely a fight of equals. This was the might of the VRS aided by armed police in an attack on villages and other places where the defenders, if armed at all, were only armed with rifles. That's the reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to Vrbanci to agree negotiations, and when I came there, I saw that people had a Zolja, which is an anti-tank weapon, and some automatic rifle, which means that they were not unarmed. I went through their barricade. I saw that they were equipped. They were armed. I spoke to Sprzo himself, the one who was subsequently killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before I show you a document to show just how unequal all of this was, were you aware of the killing of over 200 unarmed men in the Grabovica school in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Never heard that?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard of that. I don't even know where Grabovica is, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So between 1992 and today, that is the first time you're telling this Court that you ever heard of that massacre?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I'm saying. A lot of times later I heard about reports and investigations that were taking place about certain events on both sides. However, when that was going on, I didn't even know where Grabovica was. I never went to Grabovica. Not then, not later. So that's why I'm saying that I don't know where Grabovica is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just look finally then at the casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go back, please, to the document, which is at tab 31, and the number is P865. This was the report done by the inspectors on the formational activities of the Banja Luka CSB. Can we get in August of 1992. Can we go in English to page 2; and it's the -- I think it's the -- the -- the penultimate paragraph in B/C/S. So if we can highlight that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In co-operation with the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina army units, the detachment" -- mark the words "in cooperation": "The detachment participated in combat on the territory of the municipalities of the Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kupres, Kljuc, Donji Vakuf, Mrkonjic Grad, Sipovo, Derventa, Doboj, Modrica, Kotor Varos. Nine members were killed during the fighting and 25 wounded." Hardly, would you say, sir, a large casualty number?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of those nine, I believe that eight victims hailed from Kotor Varos. And that would be a lot for one unit. And for the rest, this is the standard version, as it were. I don't know that the detachment participated in those other positions. I believe that that was all before -- then things were promoted in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I was about to come on to point out to you that of that eight or nine -- sorry, nine members killed something like six or seven were killed in that one ambush that so much publicity was made about at the time. Would you agree that if they participated in that number of actions it was hardly a strong force on the other side?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, if people behave properly in conduct losses should be smaller. Because if a unit has up to 60 people and if they loss eight men, that is over 10 per cent of its entire strength. That means that something went wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I go back to where I started with my questions some days ago now. Do you consider that you have any responsibility, at all, for what happened to it the non-Serbs in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let's keep the document on the screen. It's P10394 [as interpreted]. Sir, please look at the last paragraph, or, rather, the penultimate paragraph that Ms. Korner showed you. You just told us that you didn't know that the unit participated in the areas mentioned in here and that that was before the detachment was established. Do you remember that you answered to that effect?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about that in the interview. I believe that the document was shown to you during the interview. Could you please tell me which units participated in those events and were they attached to Colonel Stevilovic?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Berets participated in those events; i.e., units that were under the direct control of Colonel Stevilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did some of the elements of those units later join the special detachment?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Since we're talking about that, could you please look at the document and tell us whether, among the municipalities where those units were active, you can see Petrovac as well?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't see Petrovac. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Please bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, a little while ago, you were shown a video. And the Prosecutor suggested that the person whom you were asked to identify was escorting a group of prisoners. Can you tell us how prisoners are escorted? How does the escort walk? Does he walk in front of the prisoners, behind the prisoners? In what manner are prisoners escorted?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually when a person is arrested or detained their hands are bound and the escort goes behind that person at a certain distance, for security reasons, the security of the person whom he is escorting, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The person that was shown to you a little while ago, was he walking in front of those persons or behind them?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in front of the group. I believe that he was first in line or maybe one step ahead of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Prosecutor showed you a concern number of documents in her examination. I would show the witness P11097, under tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I give this to the witness, please. 11091 is the document number. I apologise. 11091.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just a moment, please. The document number is P1091; I misread the number yet once again. Tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't know what you're looking at, sir. Can you look under 23, tab 23, please. Maybe you would be better off looking at the screen instead of the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not 23, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document please be zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was already shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were suggested by the Prosecutor that this is about a request for setting these individuals free. Could you please read the document carefully. It says here: "It is necessary that you release the individuals from detention and inform them to report to the Banja Luka SJB tomorrow, 21 July, for future operative steps, if necessary. In other words" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Previous translation continues] ... sorry, you ask him what he says, not what you say it says. Can't lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading Your Honours. I am reading word for word what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I apologise, it may be translation because you were being translating as saying: "In other words."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In other words, escort them to the Banja Luka basic court investigative judge."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That is exactly the complaint I was making. It is not what the document reads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The bit that he was reading: "It is necessary to release these individuals and inform them to report to the Banja Luka public security station." That's the bit that was being read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading the whole sentence. I am continuing to read -- to read the entire sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry, Your Honours, I see where he's -- I -- I thought he was reading that sentence and it's -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In other words, escort them to the Banja Luka basic court investigative judge."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, are these people requested by this document? What are they requested to do? Is this a request to liberate them or to speed up the procedure?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that this was a request to speed up the procedure. Then I went to Mr. Tutus to personally check what that was all about. When I arrived in his office and when he told me what that about, I accepted that they should be detained because there were serious accusations which were not conveyed to us properly by certain members. They thought that since they already had certain skirmishes with the police that they thought was some sort of an ploy or a set-up. And that was prosecuted, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, did you tell Mr. Zupljanin that the procedure against them was justified?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We had contact with Tutus and he told us what the situation was and they were remanded in custody. Nothing was changed in their status.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now can the witness please be shown 2D76, tab 37.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Both those questions were leading, which is why I got up originally too early, I accept. Is this is request to liberate them or speed up the procedure is a leading question. Did you tell Mr. Zupljanin that the procedure against them was justified is a leading question. In both case, the answer he got was the one that he wanted. The proper way, even in re-examination, of asking questions is in a non-leading form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see my questions as being leading. It was just an open-ended question. The question was whether something was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And whether he considered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already answered questions about that. I was interrupted when I tried to elaborate. But I said that after the conversation with Mr. Zupljanin, I went to Mr. Tutus on that occasion. So my statement does not differ from what I testified about today and that I accepted that factual situation. However, you did not want to hear the rest of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now look at tab 37 in your binder. The Prosecutor had a lot of questions about this man Boskan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ERN number in the Serbian version is 1D006407. I apologise; this is in e-court. 6047 are the last digits. It's page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, is this tab 37 in your binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor -- Prosecutor's binder. The same document but it should be page 15 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the document number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D72, page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the corner, you will find a set up of digits 1D006047. It's the same document but several pages. Look at the bottom right-hand side corner.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be zoomed in on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It will be easier for you to look at the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me. 6472.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the screen. Maybe the hard copy is not that legible.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you zoom in a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please zoom in for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What page is it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who signed the document?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djuro Bulic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we have the page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm just ... [Interpretation] Page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says in paragraph 1: "The Banja Luka SJB informed you in a dispatch that a criminal report had been filed against several members of the Banja Luka SJB special police detachment." Two persons are mentioned: Radomir Boskan and --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The security organ of the Banja Luka Corps was also informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then could you please look at the last paragraph in the same document where it -- Mr. Bulic says: "A wanted notice has been issued for Dusan Dragojevic and Radomir Boskan. If they are found --"

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "They should be arrested and taken to the Banja Luka SJB where operatives will investigate them in co-operation with the personnel of the CSB crime prevention department. Take care when making the arrest as both men are armed and they may resist the arrest."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Chief of sector."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you: Boskan and Dragojevic, were they involved in the incident?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was customary practice when somebody escapes?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A wanted notice is issued, and anybody who finds that person is duty-bound to arrest them and escort them to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Djuro Bulic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief -- or, rather, deputy to Mr. Zupljanin. It says here: "Chief of sector." And that's the police sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, let me show you one more document. In answering the Prosecutor's question about 2D0072, and the number on the document is 6041.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Page 9 in e-court. In answering the Prosecutor's questions yesterday or the day before, you spoke about official IDs, and you said that they were pure improvisation. Tell me, the name of the person on this ID, can you please read it?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Radomir Boskov.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what's the name of the person that we just spoke about? Go back to the first page of the document, page 37.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Radomir Boskan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to regular police ID documents, aren't such mistakes possible, i.e., that somebody's family name is misspelled?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is impossible. Because that person would react to such a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P567. That's tab 11; another document in the Prosecutor's binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor -- tab 11. The Prosecutor showed you this document. Could you please look at the first paragraph here. The date is 11th of May, and then the events that were described took place on the 15th of May. You have told us that you joined the unit after the parade. What was the date of the parade?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of May. That's when the Day of the Police is celebrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th, 14th, or 15th of May, were you with the unit?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only joined later. If I'd been there, I would have taken part in the parade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at exhibit -- I have a 65 ter number; 2733. It's 15A. I think you doesn't find it last time. Take a look at the end. There may be an annex, 15A. But it will also appear on the screen. I've -- I asked you a short while ago whether this unit was in the area of Petrovac. When somebody is admitted to the police, any part of the police, what is the practice when such a document is received?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you right away this document obviously didn't go through the entire procedure because once a document is received, it is stamped. It gets an entry stamp. And either the chief or some senior officer makes a note as to who it should be handed to. That's standard procedure. Alternatively, he invites one of the senior officers to talk about it. That's how it went. So if it was received regularly, it must have received an entry stamp and -- or reception stamp, and then it would have been forwarded, according to the lines of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we tell from this document whether it was received anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at document, the document at tab 12 in the Prosecution binder; P2409. You were answering the Prosecutor's questions about this document. Please read the subject line.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proposal for permanent employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please zoom in on the handwritten remarks that's beside the names. And the same in the English translation too, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an instruction. Request applications with biography and the required documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this document? What is it about?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this document is to put forward some public security employees from other areas to be received as permanent employees of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was it required for them to submit applications, CVs, and other documents?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The person who's proposing that on the left, who is that?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Dusan Rokvic who worked on defence preparations at the CSB. He was able to draft such a proposal, but he couldn't decide himself. A procedure was required for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does this procedure differ from the regular procedure to receive people into employment?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the standard procedure. [Indiscernible] application, a CV and other documents are always required, then the person is vetted and then a decision is taken. This is merely a proposal. This is nothing final. He got some sort of approval for this proposal, but there're also instructions what needs -- what still needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at Exhibit P659. It's in the Prosecution binder at tab 13. Do you have a problem with the chair?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The back of the chair is ... isn't right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you need assistance?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've a problem with my neck so maybe this can be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The same question as before. Does this document show that it was received by anybody?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at document P1096. I don't have a tab number. I don't think I have one. But it will appear on the screen. It may be tab 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor showed you this document, she put it to you that this is Stojan Zupljanin's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at it. Is this Mr. Zupljanin's signature?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It begins with an A, but I don't know whose it is. It certainly isn't Stojan's. Or maybe the first letter is Dz. But Stojan's signature begins with an S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at another document, P20323; tab 54 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I read out the 65 ter number. It's 20323. I need the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Deleted from the special detachment." And we see a list of 16 persons. Under that, there are a few more names. What does this mean, "deleted"?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that he was -- or that they were thrown out of the detachment. It was mostly due to something they -- something they did, something wrong, or due to death. But in 90 per cent of the case, it meant that the person in question was thrown out. All of these were probably thrown out of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at tab 17, please. It's P2401.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It is actually 2410. I need page -- the page with the ERN 0077432. It's the last but one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please wait a second for it to appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 65 ter number is 20317. The last-but-one page. The ERN in e-court is 0077432. Please enlarge this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The last person you talked about with Ms. Korner, Novak Zeljkovic, who was paid out pursuant to a special approval. Do you know what happened to this man, Zeljkovic? Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novak Zeljkovic died of leukemia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was he wounded?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did his injury have anything to do with his death?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was hit by a bullet with a contaminated jacket, and he developed leukemia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, could perhaps Mr. Krgovic tell me where I discussed this gentleman with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the following page of this document, the special payment for Mr. Zeljkovic. It says here: "Novak Zeljkovic was paid based on the approval given by the chief of the centre."

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, you discussed the chief's approval and asked the witness whether he spoke to Mr. Zupljanin about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P81. That's at tab 16 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you a series of questions about this document, and she then put to you that the number of killed persons was about 18. You began to answer but were interrupted. Does this document mention 18 shot people anywhere?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look where it says Nedjo Djekanovic said that: "... last night he had told Dubocanin about everything going on at the health centre and in the town and had been assured by him that it would be prevented." There any complaints or did you complain to -- to Captain Dubocanin about the conduct of his men?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While his men were a bit more relaxed when it comes to their conduct but he always shifted the blame to the Burcani. I can see from this that this may have been the reason of some reactions. We see here that Serb houses were set on fire. And talking about Dubocanin, I have already said that he a lot of influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about his men? How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the same kind of equipment as the special police. It wasn't possible to distinguish. He was able to provide stuff for them by his own connections, and most of his men had similar equipment. I've said that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We can see below that Zarko Mikic asked Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic to intervene on this occasion. Could you please comment.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably there were some problems between the units. Otherwise, he wouldn't have turned to Peulic. There was some friction between members of different structures. That's nothing unusual. Everybody boasts about themselves and slights others, and then there would also be fights among the members. That was rather widespread in military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were there mutual accusations for offences?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a common occurrence. I was able to hear several times that what I had heard before was wrong, and sometimes I was able to check and found out that it was, indeed, wrong. Other times, it was right. And when it was right, we would take people off the war-time assignment. But there was -- there were mutual accusations. You know, like children pointing fingers at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about Kotor Varos, did you ever receive a report or any information about some serious offence allegedly committed by members of the special detachment?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure when the break is due. I only want to deal with the interview with this witness, which will talk about ten minutes, so we might as well take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- if this would be convenient, Mr. Krgovic, we -- we -- I was going to -- we started a little early so I was going to take the break a little early but not quite as early as this. But this would be fine. So we rise now and come back in 20, 25 minutes. Could we go in closed session. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it then Your Honours's intention to go straight on into the next witness [overlapping speakers]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. That's what I wanted to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to an issue that you discussed with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1502 under Prosecutor's tab 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please look at the last paragraph on the page. This document is actually a report and it says that the special detachment of the police is composed of 100 members and the detachment is placed at the disposal of the 1st Krajina Corps under the command of General Talic. Can you tell me about this document? Whether, when you were in Kotor Varos during the hand-over of the unit, was it ever discussed that they should actually be transferred to the 22nd Light Assault Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that anyone ever mentioned that. It was said that they would be put under the command of General Talic. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The military police, in general terms, and special units, under whose command are they in the corps, in general terms. Do you know that? Who is their professional commander?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the military security that played the co-ordinating role in that. The very top, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when it comes to the assignment of the unit, whether it will be assigned to the command or the brigade, was that issue ever raised? Does it have anything to do with the centre? Who decided on that?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the military command, more specifically, General Talic who could decide on that if he thought that it was necessary -- necessary to issue an order for them to be sent into a unit, as far as I know. As far as I know, that was agreed, and they were transferred onto the command of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the first day of the cross-examination, the Prosecutor asked you a lot about your interview. Could you please tell me something about the course of that interview. Did you ask questions? How did it evolve?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, the questions were answered in advance. The questions were always leading. For example, did you finish that school; you were in that position at the time, weren't you, and so on and so forth. Whenever I wanted to correct something, rectify something, they would ask me something else, something different. And now that I'm -- look at the interview, I can see that the interpretation was always a bit tendentious because it turned out that the Serbs attacked the Serbs. Doesn't make too much sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you ask any questions? Did you put any questions to them?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was them all the time, that they -- that put questions to me. And effectively they tried to put answers into my mouth. I didn't accept a lot of their answers, because they did not have anything to do with logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also told you that you didn't volunteer information about your affiliation to the detachment. Please look at one part of your interview, page 48. It is P2405. The page will appear in front of you on the screen. It's at tab ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 53.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, on the first day of your testimony, you described an ARK decision to the formation of a special police detachment within the Banja Luka Security Services Centre when you said that the special-purpose police detachment was organised into platoons: Three military and one police platoon. I just wanted to clarify this. In distinguishing between military platoons and a police platoon, do you refer to where these men came from; or do you refer to functionality of the platoon?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant the personnel. The personnel came from all the different public security stations. Those were volunteers. They volunteered to join the special detachment. According to plans, the unit should have become a platoon, but I don't think that there was ever a sufficient number of men to make up a platoon, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That sort of police platoon -- you're talking now about the police platoon; right?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was a platoon which was attached to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, and a military platoon, you call it a military platoon because the members of those platoons came from the military. Did I understand that right?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a numerical indicator. Approximately three platoons or a bit more came from the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And somewhat less than one platoon came from the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But, no doubt, wherever they came from, they were all part of a police detachment, were they not?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all members of the special detachment of the CSB, the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So even the platoons that you call military platoons were, in fact, police platoons; right?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated that they were considered a special unit, de jure. De facto, it was a military unit that performed military tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm a little bit unsure about the command structure in and around the detachment. You said -- and I'm sorry, I don't have -- I don't have the exact transcript reference. I think it was on the first day of your testimony. Stevilovic was basically in charge of the operation. I think it was Vihor 92. That would be the name of the -- of the operation. The commander would be Colonel Peulic. Can you clarify for me, was Stevilovic the commander of the police detachment, or was Peulic the commander of the police detachment?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I knew, Peulic was on the ground, de jure. However, de facto, the complete operation was commanded by the security officer which -- who had more authority than General Peulic. That's how things are in the army. If somebody is a security officer, even if at a lower grade, his position is considered higher. At least that's how things were where I come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, Peulic had the title of commander of the special police detachment at a certain point in time; but Stevilovic never had that title, never that that -- well, I don't call it a rank, I call it title, he was never --

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me well. I'm talking about General Peulic. He was the commander of that Military District. Whereas, Colonel Stevilovic was, I believe, even more than that, in -- in terms of security. He had more responsibility. And all plans or activities were planned pursuant to his instructions, which means that Peulic was in a position to implement Stevilovic's instructions and nothing else. He may have had some general plans co-ordinated with the Army of Yugoslavia. I don't know any details. However, I know that there was a big problem when he killed [as interpreted] because he had all those documents and secret codes and everything of the sort with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So now I understand that Stevilovic, as well as Peulic, had broader commands than only the special detachment -- they had a special detachment under them but they were higher in the hierarchy than only commander of that special police detachment; right?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Then you said about the beating of detained persons, that they were being beaten by either the TO or the local force. What did you mean by "the local force"? The "local forces" sorry.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during that period of time, there were also men who were outside of the military composition. However, they were involved in all those activities. I know that there were men who wore civilian clothes but still carried weapons, and they participated in those activities, to bring in people. I really could not distinguish them from others. I didn't know who they belonged to. There were also those who wore all sorts of uniforms. The times were not well defined which is why practically everybody participated in those activities. When I say "everybody," I mean everybody who were in town at the time, as well as those who were not even members of any units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you include in "local forces" local police officers, local policemen?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Local policemen, reserve policemen, TO members, members of the army, members of the detachment, members who were under the command of Captain Dubocanin. Everybody who was there in town, they were all included and involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So when -- when you said that detained persons were being beaten by either TO or local forces and you included policemen, then my question would be: Did you inform anybody within the police hierarchy; and I just -- I -- I noticed that Mr. Krgovic only asked you whether you informed anybody with regard to the TO. So now I'm asking you: Did you inform anybody with regard to members of the police?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, in that building, in addition to the police, there was also the TO centre. That's where Captain Dubocanin's office was and he had a team there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Witness. Mr. Witness, will you please answer my question. It's a simple one. Did you inform anybody within the police hierarchy about policemen participating in beating detainees? Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I could not distinguish those men from each other. I didn't know who they belonged to. I'm -- I was not from that town. Second of all, I spoke about that with Captain Dubocanin. I believe that some other of his men were there. And I was told that the so-called Burcani, that was the popular name of the Territorial Defence, I was told that they simply could not be controlled - in the interpretation I heard the word "prisoners" - however, those were people who were brought into the SUP building. They were not prisoners. They were just brought in. A prisoner is somebody who is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness no need to go into that. Just one more clarification, please. Captain Dubocanin, you mentioned, he is not within the police hierarchy, is he?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. When asked by Ms. Korner about Mr. Zupljanin's request for helicopters and other equipment, your answer was: I have not seen this - the document Ms. Korner showed you - I have not seen this before, but this corroborates my version that they requested helicopters, APCs and so on, but never got any. So everything stayed the way it was, and the unit was basically taken over by the army and we were available to them for combat activities. Do you remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you saying there that, initially, the special detachment was created by the CSB as a CSB detachment and was taken over by the army only later on, after the helicopters and the other equipment initially asked for by Mr. Zupljanin were not delivered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was misunderstood, I'm afraid. I said that from the very beginning, we were, de jure, in the police, but, de facto, we were under the control of the army. And I wanted to say that this only corroborated my claim that that unit for which it was claimed previously that it had four helicopters, that that unit never had -- received four helicopters. Those stories were used only for propaganda purpose, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the beginning of your testimony, you told us that there were members of the state security centre that joined the special police detachment. Could you give a few names of -- of people from state security that were members, let's say, in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the state security?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you said in the beginning of your testimony, the first day.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That people from the state security? In the month of August? Impossible. In the month of August, that unit was already disbanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. In July then.

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the area where we were, employees of the state security were involved in some operative tasks. They were under the command of the war department, i.e., Chief of Kotor Varos State Security Department, Zdravko Mijic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The composition of the platoons and the three military and one police. I actually asked him a number of questions about that with some interruptions on the Friday, starting at page 25668. And it may well be that there's a slight contradiction now because what he said then was that although one was said to be a police platoon and the others military, because I put to him in terms, at page 25669, line 1: "You're not suggesting, sir, are you, that one part of the special police was reporting through the police chain of command and another part of the special unit was reporting through the military chain of command?" And he said: "No, they were all reporting to the military. And earlier on he said that he thought there might have been police in what is called the military platoons. So I simply put that at the moment there may be a slight contradiction. I don't know whether it's worth clarifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, I have just one clarifying question regarding a topic that we have already touched upon at several occasions during your testimony. Namely, the issue of the uniforms that were worn by the special police detachment. Because I think you testified early on that the members of the special police detachment were wearing camouflage uniforms and had blue berets. Yet all the photos that we have seen of them seem to show that they were actually wearing red berets. Are you able to clarify this or is it still the fact that sometimes they were wearing one sort of berets, and at other times, different berets. But the appearance that we have seen suggests that they were wearing red berets. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SZ-002 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The standard headwear should have been blue berets. But some of them, by private means, procured red berets. And at that time, nobody heeded official regulations much. Some people would wear berets, other, other types of hats, and different colours. Not even military units always wore helmets in theatre of war or regular hats when they were on other assignments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there anything arising from the Judges' questions? If not, Mr. Witness, we thank you for your testimony before the Tribunal. You are released, and we wish you a safe journey home. We aren't going to adjourn before the next witness comes, but we do have to go into closed session to permit the witness to be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, and can the new -- can the next witness be -- please be escorted to -- yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the next witness is brought in, we do have a small application to make. So perhaps it is better for the witness to be kept out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First of all, good afternoon Your Honours. As Ms. Korner announced before conclusion of the testimony of -- last witness, we do have an objection with relation to the next witness. Now, on Sunday, at 6.59 p.m., about seven hours after the deadline you had set for the transmission of the proofing note, we received an additional proofing note with relation to the next witness. Now, this proofing note was received following objections we raised that same afternoon about the vagueness of the -- of the first proofing note we had received. Now, the seconds proofing note includes some details but it also includes new topics. One of the new topics being the killing of prominent Serbs on the 12th of June, including Mr. Djekanovic, and a number of other named prominent Serbs. Now, first we say this is a new topic which was not included in the 65 ter summary which was filed on 28th of March, earlier this year. Secondly, we say that this is it a violation of Rule 90(H)(ii) Mr. Djekanovic was a Prosecution witness. You will remember that he testified in early 2009. And this matter was not put to him at all on a topic that we would say is quite an important topic. Following that, we had two witnesses who testified from Kotor Varos who could have dealt with this issue because the proofing note indicates that this was -- this killing reached or spread across the town of Kotor Varos generally. We had Witness ST-197 and we also had a member of the police force, ST-167. These matters could have been put to these witnesses as well. On the 12th of May, 2010, you issued a decision in relation to Rule 90(H)(ii), and at paragraph 20 you indicated there would be consequences should there be a violation of Rule 90(H)(ii). Now, you said that there will be consequences to a decision of the Defence not to put the nature of its case to a Prosecution witness. Now, at this stage, we would say that this is, as you quoted -- as you cited in the decision, a sufficiently egregious violation of the Rule. I leave it to Your Honours as to what should be done about this violation but I believe that this comes at quite a late date and this matter should have been put directly to the witness. You have two alternatives. One would be to give no value to -- to this contradiction evidence. You may also preclude the Defence from adducing this evidence. That's also part of paragraph 21 of your decision. That would be our application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Demirdjian, that you say that in our earlier decision to which you referred we went to far as to suggesting that we would preclude the side calling the witness from leading the evidence and not -- and the consequences being something other than, of course, giving little or no weight to evidence which could have been -- well, adumbrated beforehand. I appreciate that we have given a decision, but you would appreciate that sitting here several months later we can't remember the details of what we would have said, although presumably, we all have it at our breast.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We do have a copy, although it is marked, of the decision. I mean, I could read the paragraph of the decision itself if that would assist Your Honours about what was said specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That would be helpful while we are getting -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Right. Now, if I begin at paragraph 20, Your Honours say that the Trial Chamber -- I don't know if Your Honours already have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, unfortunately, we don't. So, please, if we can have it on the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Your Honours said the Trial Chamber does not consider Rule 90(H)(ii) as requiring to compel the Defence to present the nature of its case in contradiction of the evidence of Prosecution witnesses. So at that stage you decided you were not going to compel the Defence. However, you continue, the Trial Chamber holds that there will be consequences to a decision by the Defence to not put the nature of its case in contradictory to the evidence of the witness on the stand. That is paragraph 20. Now, paragraph 21, you develop also a number of matters. And you also said you will take into account the fact that the Prosecution witness was not given the opportunity to comment on the contradictory evidence. Now, again, we're talking about a witness who was here, I believe, in October or November 2009, and two years later another witness will come and testify about the fact that this person was a subject of a threat or may have been killed on the 12th of June. And you continue saying that the Trial Chamber could ascribe no probative value to contradictory Defence evidence, the nature of which was not put to the Prosecution witness while on the stand. Moreover, if the circumstances are sufficiently egregious, the Trial Chamber may preclude the Defence from adducing such contradictory evidence and avoid recalling witnesses. So this is what you decided on the 12th of May, 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding us, Mr. Demirdjian. Are you suggesting -- is it your submission that the situation with which we are faced today, that is, the, quote/unquote, sufficiently egregious set of circumstances that we anticipated?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I mean, this is an issue that is very important because we are dealing with, essentially, the president of the Crisis Staff himself who gave evidence before Your Honours. And we say this is sufficiently important in the context of the takeover. This is alleged to have happened the day after the takeover. And with respect to, again, what the Defence allege, the presence of Muslim and Croat armed forces in the municipality. This is something that should have been put to the witness while he was on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if I may link this to the first part of your objection, is it your position that you are so caught by surprise that you are practically wholly unable to deal with this in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. Had we had notice of this matter, at least when the 65 ter summary was filed on the 28th of March, we would have had sufficient time to investigate, to look into the matter. We were given this proofing note pretty much at the eleventh hour at 7.00 on Sunday night after we requested additional information. This was not even included in the first proofing note we received at 1.00 in the afternoon. So not only -- I mean, this is a brand new topic out of an additional proofing note. So, as I say, had we had enough notice, we would have been able to investigate the matter and look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, what -- why should the -- this wholly new evidence, why should you not be precluded from being able to lead this, having regard to the circumstances that Mr. Demirdjian has highlighted? That's a short question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution was informed as soon as we received the information in question. The Defence was unaware of it when it called the witness to testify and when it drafted its 65 ter summary. Only when the witness arrived in The Hague, he volunteered this information to us. At the same moment, around 1.00 on Sunday, this information was given to the OTP. The OTP requested details, and we also gave them the details a few hours later. As Ms. Korner has said several times, what the witnesses will say is a living thing. It can change and we cannot anticipate what they will say. It has happened before when -- during the OTP case, when ST-241 from Kotor Varos testified. And then we were faced with new information which was not in the 65 ter summary of the OTP; namely, that Mr. Zupljanin was at a prison somewhere. The OTP then admitted that that was new information but the -- this evidence was still allowed. The OTP can re-call the witness and request him about the circumstances. This way, the prejudice to the OTP could be remedied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- in the earlier ruling of which Mr. Demirdjian reminded us, one of the practical things that we're trying to avoid is going through the expense and inconvenience of having to re-call a witness. But faced with the situation and I -- I fully appreciate what you say about the nature of evidence and nature of witnesses is that things -- you discover things for the first time at a very late stage. But, for example, and I'm not reducing what you are saying to the absurd, if a witness -- if a witness was only on the stand and he volunteered this, he probably would have been prevented from leading that evidence. Today is Tuesday. What we are dealing with -- a situation is that just two days ago you learn of this for the first time. So my question is whether we should not simply forget about it in the same way that we would have -- had he attempted to volunteer it on the stand. Or is it your submission that this evidence is so relevant and necessary for the Trial Chamber to arrive at a just decision, that, despite the very late arrival, for want of a better expression, of this evidence you should be permitted to lead it and then we will hear what the Prosecution has to say as to how they can put themselves in a position to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is my duty as Defence counsel to represent the interests of my client to the best of my ability. To my mind, this information is essential for the understanding of the events in Kotor Varos and for the Defence of my client, as well as the whole context of the events in question. Although I learned it very late, I still must request the Trial Chamber to allow the leading of this evidence; otherwise, my client's right to a good Defence would be prejudiced. It is my duty to try to present this information which I got before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may be heard on the matter as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully agree with the words of my learned colleague, Mr. Krgovic. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of at least three situations during the -- the -- the case in-chief, where the Office of the Prosecutor produced some documents which were never given to us prior -- during the testimony of the witnesses. And then the -- the testimony of the witness was -- was heard in the court, and we were supposed to -- to prepare our cross-examination within -- overnight. And on numerous occasions, we accepted to do so, understanding that these situations are possible in cases like this. In this case, Mr. Demirdjian received the information on Sunday. He is likely to start his cross-examination probably at the end of tomorrow and continue on Thursday. So basically he will have four days to prepare his cross-examination and, therefore, it cannot be considered as -- as a totally new matter and he will have enough time to prepare with the -- prepare his cross-examination on this matter. And this is just, Your Honour -- I wanted to remind Your Honours of the standard that we had during the case in-chief, and I believe that, with all due respect, we will have to have the same standard for the Defence case as well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just one final thing on this matter. I think what Mr. Zecevic just referred to is quite a different matter in relation to adding documents to the 65 ter list or receiving them a few days in advance. This is an issue of violation of Rule 90(H)(ii) that we're referring to, having a brand new topic of their summary. Now, the problem that we're having, Your Honours, as you've -- you've noticed over and again is that we are not able to have any notice of what the witness is going to say. The first proofing note, if you've seen, it says little about the witness's evidence. It announces topics, and it is only when we request additional details that we're able to receive something, little detail here and there, but nothing that would actually put us on notice of what the witness is actually going to say. Now, it may just be that we have to call additional witnesses in rebuttal to deal with this matter if Your Honours let the witness testify to these events effectively, but effectively as Mr. Zecevic is saying that I have four days to prepare, we're talking about actually investigating this matter, not just looking in our filings or the existing evidence. If that was the case, I wouldn't rise on my feet if we already had that information. We're saying we're at a disadvantage here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We thank counsel for their indulgence.
